tribe: Banu Sa'ida of al-Khazraj — Ansar of Madina
era: The Fort That Called Out Its Dinner
teaser: His family shouted from the wall: whoever wants fat and meat, come here. He was asking Allah for money to keep it up.

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: A household that advertised its dinner to strangers
layers.content:
Sa'd ibn 'Ubada ibn Dulaym ibn Haritha, of the Banu Sa'ida of al-Khazraj. His kunya was Abu Thabit. His mother was 'Amra bint Mas'ud of the Banu an-Najjar, one of the women who gave allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ.

He could write Arabic in the Jahiliyya, when that was rare among the Arabs. He was a strong swimmer and a good archer. A man who had all three was called complete, and his people used the word of him.

But what his family was known for was not a skill. It was a shout. From the wall of their fort someone would call out across the town: whoever wants fat or meat, come to the fortress of Dulaym ibn Haritha. 'Urwa ibn az-Zubayr heard Sa'd himself making that call in his own name. Years later he heard Sa'd's son making it.

And Sa'd used to pray a prayer that would embarrass most people to say out loud. O Allah, give me praise. Give me glory. There is no glory except by acting, and no acting except with wealth. O Allah, a little will not put me right, nor can I put anything right with it.

He was asking for money because he had already decided what he would do with it.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — lineage and the description of him as 'complete'; the call from the fort and the du'a narrated from Hisham ibn 'Urwa from his father

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Three new Muslims and their own clan's idols
layers.content:
Islam reached Madina before the Prophet ﷺ did, carried by Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who had been sent ahead to recite the Qur'an and teach the deen. Sa'd was at the last 'Aqaba among the seventy Ansar, and Ibn Sa'd notes there is no disagreement about that. He was made one of the twelve leaders answerable for their people, the nine from al-Khazraj and three from al-Aws.

What happened next was not kept quiet. Muhammad ibn 'Umar records that when Sa'd ibn 'Ubada, al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr and Abu Dujana became Muslim, the three of them broke the idols of the Banu Sa'ida. Their own quarter. Their own relatives' gods.

Look at who stood with him in that. Al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr would be killed at Bi'r Ma'una. Abu Dujana would ask for the Prophet's sword at Uhud on the condition of its due. The men who pull down the family shrine are often the men who turn up later at the worst places.

For a chief of a famous house the cost was oddly specific. The fort kept feeding people. The call kept going out over the roofs. What it was calling them towards had changed.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III — 'Aqaba and the breaking of the idols of Banu Sa'ida, reported by Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Waqidi; the list of the twelve leaders also in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: A bowl every day, and one battle he never reached
layers.content:
When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madina, Sa'd sent him a bowl every single day. Meat stew, or stew with yoghurt, or with vinegar and oil, or with ghee. Ibn Sa'd says it was mostly meat. That bowl travelled with the Prophet ﷺ around the houses of his wives. When al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt lost the host they were staying with, they moved in with Sa'd and stayed until the affair of the Banu Qurayza.

Here the sources part, and it matters. Sa'd was not at Badr. He was preparing to go, and he went round the houses of the Ansar urging them out, and he was stung before he could leave, and he stayed behind. The Prophet ﷺ said of him: even if Sa'd was not present at it, he was eager for it. Some reports say he was given a share and a reward anyway. Ibn Sa'd will not let that stand unchallenged — there is no agreement on it, it is not confirmed, and none of those who catalogued the battles put his name among the men who were at Badr.

He was at Uhud, at the Ditch, and at every battle after.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III — the bowl and the guests; the account of his sting and Badr from Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Waqidi, with al-Waqidi's own note that the report of a share for him is not confirmed

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: The banner taken off him, and the day he would not raise his hand
layers.content:
On the march into Makka he carried the banner of the Ansar. Passing Abu Sufyan he called out that today would witness the great fight, that the Ka'ba would be no sanctuary, that Quraysh would be humbled. Abu Sufyan complained. The Prophet ﷺ was angry and said: no, today the Ka'ba will be honoured and Quraysh honoured. He ordered the banner taken from Sa'd and handed to his son Qays. Another version says to az-Zubayr.

After Hunayn it was Sa'd who came and told him plainly that a group of the Ansar were angry about the distribution of spoils. Asked what he himself thought, he answered: you know I am only one of them.

Then the Prophet ﷺ died, and the Ansar gathered in the roofed enclosure of the Banu Sa'ida around Sa'd, and the question of who would lead was decided over his head. 'Umar's account has Sa'd wrapped up among them, ill, while the allegiance went to Abu Bakr. When Abu Bakr later sent for his pledge, Sa'd refused: not until I have shot at you everything in my quiver.

Bashir ibn Sa'd advised leaving him alone. He is a man on his own, he said. Abu Bakr left him.
layers.source: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the banner at the conquest of Makka and Sa'd's exchange with the Prophet ﷺ after Hunayn; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the gathering of the Ansar narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab through Ibn 'Abbas and az-Zuhri, and the refusal of allegiance narrated from az-Zubayr ibn al-Mundhir as-Sa'idi

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: A well in Madina, and a fort that went quiet
layers.content:
He met 'Umar on a road outside Madina after the second caliph took office and told him, to his face, that his predecessor had been dearer to them. Then he said he would move to the neighbourhood of people better than him. He emigrated to Syria and died in Hawran, about two and a half years into 'Umar's caliphate.

How he died is strange in every telling. He was found dead, shot with two arrows, his skin turned green. Ibn Sirin's version has him say only, I feel something crawling. Madina learned of it because boys diving in a well at midday heard a voice out of the water reciting a couplet: we killed the master of Khazraj, Sa'd ibn 'Ubada, we shot him with two arrows and did not miss his heart. They remembered the day. It was the day he died.

What outlasted him was water. His mother died while the Prophet ﷺ was away and Sa'd asked what sadaqa was best to give for her. Making water flow, he was told. Al-Hasan, generations later, was asked whether a man could drink from the water in the mosque. Abu Bakr and 'Umar drank from it, he said. It is the water of Umm Sa'd.

And 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar once sent a boy to listen at the old fort for anyone calling people to dinner. There was no one. You spoke the truth, he said.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III — the exchange with 'Umar and the death in Hawran narrated from Yahya ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Sa'id ibn Sa'd; the couplet from the well from 'Abd al-'Aziz and from Muhammad ibn Sirin; the sadaqa of water narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab through Qatada, and al-Hasan's answer from Suwayd Abu Hatim

quiz.prompt: Why was Sa'd ibn Ubadah not present at Badr?

options.text: He was left in charge of Madina
He was stung while going round the houses of the Ansar urging them to go out
He had not yet become Muslim
He was away trading in Syria

quiz.citation: Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Waqidi — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ said of him that even though Sa'd was not present at it, he was eager for it. Ibn Sa'd is careful to add that reports giving him a share of the spoils are not confirmed.

quiz.prompt: What happened when Sa'd, carrying the banner of the Ansar into Makka, announced that Quraysh would be humbled that day?

options.text: The Prophet ﷺ repeated the words after him
Abu Sufyan surrendered on the spot
The banner was taken from him and given to his son Qays
He was sent back to Madina

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the conquest of Makka
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ answered him with the opposite sentence: today the Ka'ba is honoured and Quraysh is honoured. Another version of the report gives the banner to az-Zubayr rather than to Qays.

quiz.prompt: What did Sa'd send to the Prophet ﷺ every day after he arrived in Madina?

options.text: A bowl of stew, mostly meat, which travelled round the houses of his wives
A written report on the affairs of al-Khazraj
A share of the date harvest
Two of his own sons to serve him

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Sometimes it was stew with yoghurt, sometimes vinegar and oil, sometimes ghee. Ibn Sa'd notes it was mostly meat, which in that town was the expensive answer.

quiz.prompt: When Abu Bakr sent asking for his allegiance after the Prophet ﷺ died, what did Sa'd say?

options.text: He gave it immediately and publicly
He asked for a month to think
He refused, saying not until he had shot everything in his quiver
He said he would follow whatever al-Khazraj decided

quiz.citation: Narrated from az-Zubayr ibn al-Mundhir as-Sa'idi — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Bashir ibn Sa'd advised Abu Bakr to leave him be, because he was a man on his own and would harm nothing. Abu Bakr accepted the advice. Nobody came for him.

quiz.prompt: Sa'd asked the Prophet ﷺ which charity was best to give on behalf of his dead mother. What was the answer?

options.text: Freeing a slave
Making water flow
Feeding forty poor men
Building a mosque in her name

quiz.citation: Narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab through Qatada — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Generations later al-Hasan was asked whether it was permitted to drink the water in the mosque. He answered that Abu Bakr and 'Umar had drunk from it, and that it was the water of Umm Sa'd.

quiz.prompt: Sa'd prayed out loud for wealth, on the stated grounds that he could not accomplish anything without it. What is your honest relationship with money as a tool?

options.text: I am uneasy asking for it, even for good ends
I ask for it and I am vague about what I would do with it
I have a specific plan and not enough means
I have means and no plan, and that bothers me

quiz.citation: The du'a narrated from Hisham ibn 'Urwa from his father — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His prayer named the mechanism: no glory except by acting, no acting except with wealth. He was not asking for comfort. He was asking for capacity.

quiz.prompt: His family's generosity was announced from a wall, by name, for the whole town to hear. Where do you sit on giving that people can see?

options.text: I only feel clean about it if nobody knows
Being seen keeps me consistent, and I know that
I let it be seen and then feel uncomfortable afterwards
I mostly give when asked, and rarely announce anything

quiz.citation: The call from the fort, narrated from 'Urwa ibn az-Zubayr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The call was inherited. His father's fort made it, then Sa'd made it in his own name, then his son made it. Something publicly repeated is harder to quietly drop.

quiz.prompt: He was preparing for Badr, urging others to go, and a sting kept him home. How do you carry being absent from something you genuinely wanted?

options.text: I explain myself more than anyone asked me to
I quietly assume people think less of me
I trust that the wanting counted and let it go
I overcompensate at the next opportunity

quiz.citation: The Prophet's ﷺ words on Sa'd and Badr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ named his eagerness rather than his absence. And Ibn Sa'd still refused to write him into the roll of Badr, because he was not there. Both things were allowed to be true.

quiz.prompt: One sentence on the road into Makka cost him the banner, in front of the whole army. How do you receive correction that arrives publicly?

options.text: I accept it and privately rehearse the injustice of it for days
I would rather be corrected publicly than talked about privately
The audience is the part I cannot get past
I go quiet, and the lesson does land eventually

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the conquest of Makka
quiz.scholar_reflection: The banner went to his own son. He was not removed from the march or from the trust, only from the sentence he had just said.

quiz.prompt: Rather than pledge something he did not believe, he told 'Umar to his face that Abu Bakr had been dearer, and moved away. Where is your line between loyalty and honesty?

options.text: I say the agreeable thing and resent myself later
I say the true thing and lose relationships over it
I withdraw rather than argue, and call that peace
It depends entirely on how much power the other person has

quiz.citation: Narrated from Yahya ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Sa'id ibn Sa'd — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said he was not one to pretend. He also did not raise a hand or gather his tribe. He removed himself from the room instead, and he paid for that with exile.
